title: Why "Pressure Passes" Are A Ridiculous Behavior Strategy
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin sharply criticizes 'pressure passes' -- slips that let difficult students leave class on demand -- as an administrator-driven accommodation that looks like action while avoiding any real accountability. He lays out five concrete failure modes: students miss instructional time, students who are prone to misbehavior will exploit the pass rather than use it earnestly, unsupervised students outside the classroom create liability and safety risks, the passes embolden further disruption once students realize consequences aren't coming, and the passes send a self-fulfilling message that a student can't control themselves. He draws a sharp distinction between this blanket policy and a genuinely prepared, individualized accommodation he once used for a student with real panic attacks, arguing that removing structure and accountability, rather than addressing root behavioral or emotional issues, ultimately harms the students it claims to help.
points: Pressure passes that let students leave class on demand are argued to cause missed instruction, exploitation by misbehaving students, and safety liability from lack of supervision.
Unsupervised students outside the classroom are framed as a serious liability risk, not just a management inconvenience.
The policy sends students the self-fulfilling message that they can't control themselves, which can follow them long-term.
A genuinely prepared, individualized accommodation for a student with real panic attacks is contrasted with the blanket pressure-pass policy as the legitimate alternative.
quotes: They’re slips of red or yellow paper that allow difficult students to leave your classroom anytime they like. Yep, they just flash you the pass and then walk out.
Students who have a proclivity to misbehave aren’t going to use a pressure pass earnestly. It’s naive to think otherwise.
Students can never, ever be left unsupervised. Picture yourself on the witness stand. “Well, I just assumed he’d stay right there.
By allowing a student to leave when they feel the need, you’re very effectively telling them that they can’t control themselves.
We’re talking about giving up on students who desperately need fair, consistent, and tough-loved accountability.
